title: Dependency and Action Supply-Chain Security
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of dependency and action supply-chain security and identify when it should be used.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on dependency and action supply-chain security. Supply-chain safety includes reviewing third-party actions, pinning them to full commit SHAs, tracking dependencies, and monitoring security updates. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Dependency and Action Supply-Chain Security matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Supply-chain safety includes reviewing third-party actions, pinning them to full commit SHAs, tracking dependencies, and monitoring security updates. Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Supply-chain safety includes reviewing third-party actions, pinning them to full commit SHAs, tracking dependencies, and monitoring security updates. Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Minimizing third-party dependencies
items.text: Use a scoped token, validate request inputs and event payloads, check HTTP/error status, handle pagination and rate limits, and avoid logging credentials or unneeded private response data.

items.title: Monitoring vulnerable dependencies
items.text: Start with the first failed step and its exit code, then inspect the event, conditions, permissions, tool versions, network, and runner state. Capture sanitized diagnostics and preserve evidence of the failure.

content_blocks.code:
name: Review action dependencies
on: pull_request
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4 # readable example only; production should use a reviewed full commit SHA
      - run: echo "Review action source, permissions, release process, and dependency updates"

troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
